Riches
RICH-ez
n. (pl.)
From Old French richesse, “wealth, opulence,” from riche (rich). Renders the Greek ploutos, “wealth, riches,” both literal and (chiefly in Paul) of the spiritual riches given in Christ; and the Hebrew ‘ōsher, “riches.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Riches in Scripture have a material register and a spiritual register, and Paul especially exploits the second to set forth the gospel’s great gifts. Material riches are treated soberly: they are gifts of God when given (the wealth of Abraham, Job, Solomon was from the LORD), they are dangers when held wrongly (they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare; how hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!), they are to be enjoyed with thanksgiving and held with open hands ready to do good and to communicate (1 Tim 6:17-19), and they are nothing in the day of wrath (their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD). The deeper biblical riches—the riches that the New Testament most loves to celebrate—are the spiritual riches given in Christ. Paul names them in tight, jewel-like phrases: the riches of his grace (Eph 1:7; 2:7), the riches of his glory (Rom 9:23; Eph 3:16; Phil 4:19; Col 1:27), the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints (Eph 1:18), the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom 11:33), the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering (Rom 2:4), and the unsearchable riches of Christ (Eph 3:8). The cumulative effect is staggering: God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and the very person of His Son are all, in apostolic vocabulary, riches—wealth bestowed on the church, an inheritance reserved in heaven, a treasure that exceeds every earthly treasure precisely because it cannot be taken away. The supreme contrast text is 2 Cor 8:9: for ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. The Son’s self-impoverishment in the incarnation is the means by which the spiritually bankrupt are made spiritually rich in Him. The saint’s relation to riches is therefore two-edged. He holds material riches lightly when given, generously when shared, and not at all as the measure of his security; and he holds the spiritual riches of Christ as his actual treasure, his unfading inheritance, his exhaustless storehouse, the wealth that no thief breaks through to steal and no rust corrupts.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines RICHES as wealth; opulence; affluence; possessions of land, goods, or money in abundance; figuratively, splendid, sumptuous, or expensive things; in scripture, the spiritual blessings and treasures given in Christ.

expand to see more

RICHES, n. pl. — 1. Wealth; opulence; affluence; possessions of land, goods, or money in abundance. 2. That which makes rich, as moral or spiritual qualities. 3. Splendid, sumptuous, or expensive things. 4. In scripture, the spiritual blessings and treasures given in Christ; as, the unsearchable riches of Christ (Eph 3:8); the riches of his grace (Eph 1:7); the riches of his glory (Phil 4:19).

RICH, a. — 1. Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods, or money. 2. In scripture, abounding in spiritual gifts; abounding in grace and divine favor.

📖 Key Scripture

Ephesians 1:7 — "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace."

Ephesians 3:8 — "Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ."

Philippians 4:19 — "But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus."

2 Corinthians 8:9 — "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Biblical riches are corrupted by the materialist register of the present age that has trained the believer to feel the word as referring chiefly to money—and by the prosperity gospel’s further confusion that uses the apostolic riches-of-Christ language as the warrant for promising material prosperity to the faithful.

expand to see more

The materialist register of late-modern consumer culture has trained the believer to hear riches as referring chiefly to money, and to read even the apostolic phrases through that lens. Paul’s riches of his grace, riches of his glory, unsearchable riches of Christ, and Philippians 4:19’s my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus, ought to evoke in the saint the staggering wealth of what God has bestowed and reserved in Christ; they often evoke, in the contemporary register, vague hopes of financial provision. Recover the doctrine, and the apostolic phrases recover their proper weight. The riches Paul celebrates are God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and the very person of His Son—treasures the believer can savor with his eyes closed and his bank account empty, and that survive every loss the present life can bring.

The prosperity gospel takes the cultural materialism a step further and uses the apostolic riches-of-Christ language as the warrant for promising material prosperity to the faithful. The verses are quoted; the substitution is performed; the spiritual riches Paul means are conflated with the financial riches the prosperity gospel promises; and the believer is taught to expect that his union with Christ entitles him to material flourishing in this life. Scripture refuses the substitution. Christ Himself had no place to lay His head; the apostles for the most part died in poverty and martyrdom; the saints of Hebrews 11 wandered in deserts; the Macedonian saints’ deep poverty is celebrated alongside the riches of their liberality. The spiritual riches of Christ are real and exhaustless, but they are spiritual—the riches that no thief breaks through to steal—and they do not translate into a divine guarantee of material wealth in this life. Recover both ends. Hold the spiritual riches of Christ in their full apostolic weight; receive material provision with thanksgiving as a gift; hold it with open hands; refuse to confuse the two.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ploutos (wealth, riches) and the verb ploutiō (to enrich); Hebrew ‘ōsher (riches)—both material wealth (gift when given, danger when held wrongly) and the spiritual riches of God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and very person bestowed in Christ.

expand to see more

Greek ploutos (G4149) — wealth, riches (used by Paul of the riches of God’s grace, glory, wisdom).

Greek plousios (G4145) — rich, wealthy (the adjective; 2 Cor 8:9, “though he was rich”).

Greek ploutiō (G4147) — to make rich, enrich (2 Cor 8:9, “that ye through his poverty might be rich”).

Hebrew ‘ōsher (H6239) — riches, wealth (Gen 31:16; Eccl 4:8; Jer 17:11).

Usage

"The riches Paul celebrates are God’s grace, glory, wisdom, goodness, and the very person of His Son—treasures the saint can savor with empty hands and full heart."

"Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich—the Son’s self-impoverishment is the means by which the bankrupt are enriched."

"Materialism reduces riches to money; prosperity gospel conflates spiritual riches with material wealth; biblical doctrine holds both registers in their proper distinct places."
